metadata.note: Roanoke, Virginia as a passenger rail hub, and the Norfolk & Western lines that made it one. Roanoke was the village of Big Lick until the Norfolk & Western - reorganized out of the Atlantic, Mississippi & Ohio in 1881 - put its headquarters and shops there and the Shenandoah Valley Railroad came down the valley to meet it in 1882. Four routes are drawn: the 408-mile main line Norfolk-Petersburg-Lynchburg-Roanoke-Bristol (with its three predecessors drawn separately from the years they opened - South Side 1854, Virginia & Tennessee to Big Lick 1852 and on to Bristol 1856, Norfolk & Petersburg 1858 - then the AM&O 1870-1881 and N&W 1881-1971); the Shenandoah Valley line north to Hagerstown (1882-1963); the Punkin Vine south to Winston-Salem (1892-1961); and the Blacksburg Branch, the 'Huckleberry' (1904-1958). In 1898, the year this layer was built to answer, Roanoke had all of the first three; Blacksburg had no railroad at all - the Huckleberry did not reach it until September 1904, and until then Blacksburg's station was the N&W at Cambria, four miles away. Each feature is split at its ownership changes so colour tracks who ran the trains (Rule 4). Geometry is real OpenStreetMap trace; headways throughout are estimates, not timetable readings.
not_yet_sourced: every headway in this layer is an editorial estimate; no Official Guide or N&W public timetable was consulted for any era
the end of Shenandoah Division passenger service: 10 June 1962 (Railfan & Railroad) vs a through sleeper to 27 October 1962 and a local into February 1963 (Wikipedia). Drawn to 1963
the 1930 and 1922 era splits inside several features are editorial, chosen to separate the named-train peak from the decline, not documented transition dates
Amtrak's Mountaineer (1975-1977) and Hilltopper (1977-1979) ran over this main line through Roanoke and are NOT drawn here - they continued far west of Bristol/Bluefield and belong in an Amtrak layer
the Virginian Railway, which reached Roanoke in 1909 and carried passengers until 1956, is not drawn in this layer
metadata.geometry_note: All four routes are traced on today's Norfolk Southern alignment. That is the same corridor throughout, but N&W eased and relocated stretches of the main line after 1900, so the 1850s-1880s features are drawn on a later line than their own trains used - most visibly on the Christiansburg mountain crossing and the New River approach to Radford. Traced against documented mileage: main line 401.3 mi drawn / 408 documented; Shenandoah 237.5 / 238; Punkin Vine 120.4 / ~122; Blacksburg Branch 8.3 / 8.75.

segments.note: Opened for through service 1 September 1858, William Mahone's line from Norfolk to Petersburg, carrying passengers as well as the Norfolk-bound traffic of the connecting South Side and Virginia & Tennessee. Service was disrupted and the line heavily damaged during the Civil War; that interruption is not modelled here. Independent operation ended 12 November 1870 when the N&P was consolidated into the Atlantic, Mississippi & Ohio. Frequency estimated - no 1850s-60s timetable was consulted.
sources: Segment-level: the 1 September 1858 opening and the 12 November 1870 AM&O consolidation are from the N&WHS corporate timeline and the Wikipedia articles; the headway is an estimate and is not sourced.

segments.note: The South Side Railroad was completed in 1854 from City Point through Petersburg to Lynchburg, where it interchanged with the Virginia & Tennessee. Only the Petersburg-Lynchburg portion, the piece that became the N&W main line, is drawn. Consolidated into the Atlantic, Mississippi & Ohio on 12 November 1870. Frequency estimated.

segments.note: The first V&T train reached Big Lick - the village that became Roanoke - on 1 November 1852, four years before the railroad was finished to Bristol. This 52-mile piece is drawn from that date because it opened first. Consolidated into the Atlantic, Mississippi & Ohio on 12 November 1870. Frequency estimated.

properties.geometry_quality: real-traced from OpenStreetMap: the Norfolk Southern districts that are the original N&W main line (Norfolk District, Blue Ridge District, Whitethorne/Christiansburg Districts, Pulaski District), assembled by corridor-constrained shortest path through Petersburg, Lynchburg, Roanoke and Bristol. 401.3 mi traced against 408 mi documented Norfolk-Bristol. No straight-line approximation over 1 mi. Two gaps account for the shortfall: the trace stops 0.8 mi short of the N&W's Norfolk terminal station site (that trackage is lifted), and at Petersburg it follows the through alignment, passing about 2.3 mi south of Petersburg Union Station rather than running into it (the station stub survives in OSM only as an out-and-back spur and was trimmed). ERA WARNING: this is today's alignment. N&W rebuilt and eased much of the main line after 1900 - the Elliston-Christiansburg mountain crossing and the Merrimac grade in particular - so the 1850s-1880s features drawn on it follow a later line than the one their trains actually used. Straight-line repair 2026-08-29: 1 ruled segment totalling 53 mi replaced with OpenStreetMap-traced rail geometry (see geometry_repairs for the OSM lines each one followed).

segments.note: Formed 12 November 1870 by consolidating the Norfolk & Petersburg, South Side and Virginia & Tennessee into one 408-mile railroad from Norfolk to Bristol, under William Mahone, with headquarters at Lynchburg. Sold under foreclosure on 9 February 1881 to E. W. Clark & Co. and renamed the Norfolk & Western. Frequency estimated.
sources: Segment-level: the 12 November 1870 consolidation, the 408-mile Norfolk-Bristol figure and the 9 February 1881 foreclosure sale are from the N&WHS corporate timeline and Wikipedia; the headway is an estimate and is not sourced.

segments.note: The Atlantic, Mississippi & Ohio became the Norfolk & Western Railroad on 9 February 1881. The new company moved its shops and headquarters to the junction village of Big Lick, renamed Roanoke in 1882, and the town went from a few hundred people to a railroad city. Union Station, between the N&W and Shenandoah Valley tracks in front of the Hotel Roanoke, opened in 1882. Frequency estimated.
sources: Segment-level: the 1881 renaming and the move to Roanoke are from the N&WHS timeline and Wikipedia; the 1882 Union Station is from the Roanoke station article. The headway is an estimate and is not sourced.

segments.note: Reorganized as the Norfolk & Western Railway in 1896. This is the era the map's 1898 view shows: Roanoke as the system's headquarters and main terminal, with the main line east to Norfolk and west to Bristol, the Shenandoah Valley line north to Hagerstown and the Winston-Salem line south all meeting there. The present Roanoke depot opened on the site of the 1882 station on 29 June 1905. Frequency estimated - no Official Guide page was consulted for this era.
sources: NOT SOURCED AT SEGMENT LEVEL: the 1896 reorganization and the 1905 depot are sourced, but the 1898 service level behind this headway is not - nobody has checked a timetable for it.

segments.note: The named-train era: the Pocahontas (Norfolk-Cincinnati), the Cavalier and, from 1946, the streamlined Powhatan Arrow, all of them calling at Roanoke; and, west of Lynchburg, the Southern Railway's Birmingham Special, Tennessean and Pelican, which N&W hauled over its own rails between Lynchburg and Bristol. Frequency estimated.
sources: NOT SOURCED AT SEGMENT LEVEL: the trains named here are documented, but the 1930-1958 split and the headway are editorial and unsourced.

segments.note: Postwar decline. The Tennessean ended in 1968, the Powhatan Arrow on 23 May 1969, the Birmingham Special lost its name in February 1970 and was cut back to Bristol that August. N&W declined to join Amtrak, so all of it ended together: the last Pocahontas ran on 30 April 1971, the eve of Amtrak's first day, and with it passenger service over the whole Norfolk-Bristol main line. Frequency estimated.
sources: Segment-level: the 1968 Tennessean, 23 May 1969 Powhatan Arrow, February/August 1970 Birmingham Special and 30 April 1971 final Pocahontas are from the Roanoke station, Pocahontas and Birmingham Special articles; the headway is an estimate and is not sourced.

segments.note: Completed 19 June 1882 up the Shenandoah Valley from Hagerstown, Maryland through the West Virginia panhandle and down the Virginia valley through Front Royal, Luray, Waynesboro and Buena Vista to Roanoke, where it met the N&W. Its arrival is what turned Big Lick into a junction and made Roanoke worth building shops at. Sold under foreclosure in September 1890 and absorbed by the Norfolk & Western that December. Frequency estimated.
sources: Segment-level: the 19 June 1882 completion and the December 1890 absorption into N&W are from the Wikipedia Shenandoah Valley Railroad article and the N&WHS timeline; the headway is an estimate and is not sourced.

segments.note: N&W absorbed the Shenandoah Valley Railway in December 1890, giving Roanoke a northern outlet through Hagerstown to the Pennsylvania Railroad at Harrisburg and on to New York. Frequency estimated.
sources: NOT SOURCED AT SEGMENT LEVEL: the December 1890 absorption is sourced; the 1930 split and the headway are editorial and unsourced.

segments.note: Two trains a day each way into the mid-century, N&W numbers 1 and 2 running Roanoke-New York via Hagerstown and Harrisburg as a pooled overnight train with the Pennsylvania Railroad. SOURCE CONFLICT on the ending: Railfan & Railroad gives the end of the through service as 10 June 1962, while the Roanoke station article has the through sleeper ending 27 October 1962 and a local surviving into February 1963. Drawn to 1963, the latest of the three.
sources: Segment-level: the pooled N&W/PRR Roanoke-New York service and the conflicting 1962/1963 end dates are from the Railfan & Railroad piece on the Shenandoah Valley Railroad and the Wikipedia Roanoke station article; the headway is an estimate and is not sourced.

segments.note: The Roanoke & Southern - the 'Punkin Vine' - was completed from Roanoke to Winston-Salem in 1892 and leased to the N&W as soon as it opened, so it is drawn in N&W colours from the start (Rule 4); N&W bought it outright in 1896. It gave Roanoke a southern outlet and Winston-Salem's tobacco trade a northern one. Frequency estimated.
sources: Segment-level: the 1892 completion and immediate N&W lease, and the 1896 purchase, are from the N&WHS corporate timeline; the headway is an estimate and is not sourced.

segments.note: Reduced to a single daily round trip, trains 11 and 12, in its last decades. The last Punkin Vine passenger train ran on 18 February 1961. Freight continued over the line, which is still an NS district today - that is context, not drawn service. Frequency estimated.
sources: Segment-level: the 18 February 1961 last run of trains 11/12 is from the Wikipedia Roanoke station article; the 1930 split and the headway are estimates and are not sourced.

properties.geometry_quality: part-traced, part rail-trail: real-traced from OpenStreetMap ways tagged old_railway_operator=N&W - the surviving NS Blacksburg Branch out of Cambria and, north of it, the abandoned grade now carried by the Huckleberry Trail. 8.3 mi traced against 8.75 mi documented Christiansburg-Blacksburg. One straight-line approximation: 0.8 mi across the built-over grade on the south side of Blacksburg, between the end of the mapped grade at Merrimac Road and its resumption near Blacksburg Middle School. The north end stops 0.2 mi short of the Blacksburg depot site at Draper Road; the modern trail's realigned loops around Hethwood are deliberately not followed.

segments.note: The Virginia Anthracite Coal & Railway built this line in 1902 to bring coal from its Merrimac mines down to the N&W at Cambria, and extended it into Blacksburg in 1904 under a contract with Virginia Agricultural & Mechanical College. The first passenger train ran into Blacksburg on 15 September 1904 with free rides for the town - before that Blacksburg had no railroad, and passengers used the N&W at Cambria. The 1902-1904 coal-only years are deliberately not drawn (Rule 1). The company failed and was sold under foreclosure to the N&W in 1911. Frequency estimated.
sources: Segment-level: the 1902 founding, the 1904 extension, the 15 September 1904 first passenger train and the foreclosure sale are from the N&W Historical Society Radford Division page, the Friends of the Huckleberry Trail history and Virginia Tech Magazine; the headway is an estimate and is not sourced.

Same geometry as the Virginia Anthracite feature it succeeds.

segments.note: N&W took ownership in January 1912 and ran the line as its Blacksburg Branch, 8.75 miles from Christiansburg, beginning at milepost 290.0 from Norfolk. Four runs a day, three of them carrying mail; from 1912 to 1922 the Huckleberry was Blacksburg's main link to the outside world, with three runs a day carrying 50 to 60 passengers each. It was slow enough that the story of picking huckleberries alongside the moving train stuck as its name.
sources: Segment-level: the January 1912 N&W takeover, the 8.75-mile length, milepost 290.0 and the four-runs-a-day / 1912-1922 traffic figures are from the N&W Historical Society Radford Division page, Virginia Tech Magazine and the Friends of the Huckleberry Trail history.

segments.note: Declining as paved roads and buses reached Blacksburg. The last passenger train unloaded its riders in August 1958; the last freight ran into Blacksburg on 30 June 1966 and the line north of Peppers Ferry Road was abandoned in the 1960s - freight and abandonment are context, not drawn service (Rule 1). The grade is now the Huckleberry Trail. Frequency estimated.
sources: Segment-level: the August 1958 last passenger train and the 30 June 1966 last freight are from Virginia Tech Magazine and the Friends of the Huckleberry Trail history; the 1922 split and the headway are estimates and are not sourced.
